description:
A geared bronze machine that predicted eclipses existed in the ancient world about two thousand years ago. Sponge divers found the wreck off Antikythera in 1900, recovered the corroded lump in 1901, and its fragments are now held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. What survives is 82 fragments containing 30 bronze gear wheels. The mechanism was built around 100 BCE. Nothing comparably complex appears again for about 1,400 years, until the great clocks of medieval cathedrals. No inscription names its builder, and no ancient text describes the workshop that made it or the person who paid for it.

The evidence is what we have. The unanswered questions are what remain. What do you think happened? What does the record actually support?

Sources you can check:
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Antikythera mechanism": https://www.britannica.com/topic/Antikythera-mechanism
- Freeth et al., Nature 2006, "Decoding the ancient Greek astronomical calculator known as the Antikythera Mechanism": https://doi.org/10.1038/nature05357
- Freeth et al., Scientific Reports 2021, "A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism": https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-84310-w
- National Archaeological Museum, Athens, Collection of Metalwork: https://www.namuseum.gr/en/permanent_exhibition/erga-metallotechnias/
- The Sea, "Antikythera Mechanism Discovery: How It Was Decoded": https://thesea.org/antikythera-mechanism-one-amazing-discovery/
- Efstathiou et al., Heritage 2021, "The Antikythera Mechanism: The Prove of the Accuracy of the Astronomical Calculations Based on It": https://doi.org/10.3390/heritage4040211 (supports the inscription research in the full long-form; the inscription-count claim is not narrated in this Short)

Unsolved history and mysteries from around the world, investigated with modern tech — lost cities, events nobody can fully explain, and artifacts that shouldn't exist, reconstructed and tested with today's tools.

Full deep dive: The 2,000-Year-Old Object That Shouldn't Exist (The Deep Scan long-form, YouTube k_wGkEfT5QI).
